questions.question: Write a query to compute pipeline SLA — what percentage of partitions loaded on time.

blocks.source:
WITH runs AS (
  SELECT DATE(partition_date) AS pdate, MIN(completed_at) AS first_complete,
    DATE_TRUNC('day', MIN(completed_at)) + INTERVAL '8 hours' AS sla_deadline
  FROM pipeline_run_log WHERE status='success' GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT pdate, first_complete, sla_deadline,
  CASE WHEN first_complete <= sla_deadline THEN 'MET' ELSE 'MISSED' END AS sla_status,
  ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (first_complete-sla_deadline))/60, 1) AS mins_vs_sla
FROM runs ORDER BY pdate DESC;

questions.question: Write a master pipeline health dashboard query — freshness, volume, SLA, and status in one.

blocks.source:
SELECT p.pipeline_name, p.status, p.last_run_at, p.records_processed,
  ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW()-p.last_run_at))/3600,1) AS hours_since_run,
  ROUND(100.0*p.records_processed/NULLIF(
    AVG(p.records_processed) OVER (PARTITION BY p.pipeline_name ORDER BY p.last_run_at ROWS 7 PRECEDING)
  ,0),1) AS pct_of_7d_avg,
  CASE
    WHEN p.status != 'success' THEN 'FAILED'
    WHEN EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW()-p.last_run_at))/3600 > p.sla_hours THEN 'SLA BREACH'
    WHEN p.records_processed < AVG(p.records_processed) OVER (PARTITION BY p.pipeline_name ORDER BY p.last_run_at ROWS 7 PRECEDING) * 0.5 THEN 'LOW VOLUME'
    ELSE 'HEALTHY'
  END AS health
FROM pipeline_run_log p
WHERE p.last_run_at = (SELECT MAX(last_run_at) FROM pipeline_run_log p2 WHERE p2.pipeline_name=p.pipeline_name)
ORDER BY health DESC;

questions.question: What is the difference between a full refresh and incremental model in dbt? When to use each?

blocks.html: Full refresh — drops and rebuilds the entire table on every run. Simple, always correct, no watermark logic needed. Use for: small tables, dimensions, tables where historical data can change.

Incremental — only processes new/changed records. Much faster for billions of rows. Use for: large append-only fact tables, event logs. Risk: bugs are hard to correct retroactively without backfilling.

questions.question: Write a query to assign new surrogate keys to incoming dimension records.

blocks.source:
WITH max_key AS (SELECT COALESCE(MAX(customer_key),0) AS mk FROM dim_customer),
     new_recs AS (
       SELECT s.* FROM staging_customers s
       LEFT JOIN dim_customer d ON s.customer_id=d.customer_id AND d.is_current=TRUE
       WHERE d.customer_id IS NULL
     )
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_key, customer_id, name, email, eff_from, is_current)
SELECT mk.mk + ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY nr.customer_id), nr.customer_id, nr.name, nr.email, CURRENT_DATE, TRUE
FROM new_recs nr, max_key mk;

questions.question: Write a funnel analysis query — calculate drop-off at each stage of a user funnel.

blocks.source:
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step >= 1 THEN user_id END) AS visited_homepage,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step >= 2 THEN user_id END) AS viewed_product,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step >= 3 THEN user_id END) AS added_to_cart,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step >= 4 THEN user_id END) AS purchased,
  ROUND(100.0*COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step>=2 THEN user_id END)/NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step>=1 THEN user_id END),0),1) AS step1_to_2_pct,
  ROUND(100.0*COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step>=3 THEN user_id END)/NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step>=2 THEN user_id END),0),1) AS step2_to_3_pct,

questions.question: Write a retention cohort query — what % of users are still active 7, 14, 30 days after signup.

blocks.source:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('week', signup_date) AS cohort_week FROM users
),
activity AS (
  SELECT e.user_id, c.cohort_week,
    DATE_DIFF('day', c.cohort_week, DATE_TRUNC('day', e.event_time)) AS day_num
  FROM events e JOIN cohort c ON e.user_id=c.user_id
),
cohort_size AS (SELECT cohort_week, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS sz FROM cohort GROUP BY 1)
SELECT a.cohort_week, cs.sz AS cohort_size,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN day_num BETWEEN 1 AND 7   THEN a.user_id END) AS retained_d7,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN day_num BETWEEN 1 AND 14  THEN a.user_id END) AS retained_d14,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN day_num BETWEEN 1 AND 30  THEN a.user_id END) AS retained_d30,
  ROUND(100.0*COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN day_num BETWEEN 1 AND 7 THEN a.user_id END)/cs.sz,1) AS d7_pct
FROM activity a JOIN cohort_size cs ON a.cohort_week=cs.cohort_week
GROUP BY a.cohort_week, cs.sz ORDER BY a.cohort_week;

questions.question: Write a query to compute 7-day, 28-day, and 90-day active users (DAU/WAU/MAU) in one query.

blocks.source:
SELECT event_date,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)                                              AS dau,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_date - e2.event_date < 7  THEN e2.user_id END) AS wau,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_date - e2.event_date < 28 THEN e2.user_id END) AS mau_28d
FROM events e
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT user_id, event_date FROM events e2 WHERE e2.event_date <= e.event_date) e2
GROUP BY event_date;

-- More efficient version
SELECT d.date,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_date = d.date THEN e.user_id END) AS dau,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_date BETWEEN d.date-6 AND d.date THEN e.user_id END) AS wau,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_date BETWEEN d.date-27 AND d.date THEN e.user_id END) AS mau
FROM dim_date d JOIN events e ON e.event_date BETWEEN d.date-27 AND d.date
GROUP BY d.date ORDER BY d.date;

questions.question: Write a query to compute session-level metrics: duration, pages per session, and bounce rate.

blocks.source:
WITH sessions AS (
  SELECT session_id, user_id,
    MIN(event_time) AS session_start,
    MAX(event_time) AS session_end,
    COUNT(*) AS page_views
  FROM page_view_events GROUP BY session_id, user_id
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_sessions,
  ROUND(AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (session_end-session_start))/60), 2) AS avg_duration_min,
  ROUND(AVG(page_views), 2) AS avg_pages_per_session,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN page_views=1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*), 2) AS bounce_rate_pct
FROM sessions
WHERE session_start >= CURRENT_DATE-7;

questions.question: Write an A/B test results query — calculate conversion rate and statistical significance.

blocks.source:
WITH experiment AS (
  SELECT
    variant,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)    AS users,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN converted=1 THEN user_id END) AS conversions
  FROM ab_test_events WHERE experiment_id='checkout_v2'
  GROUP BY variant
)
SELECT
  variant, users, conversions,
  ROUND(100.0*conversions/NULLIF(users,0), 3) AS conversion_rate_pct,
  -- Z-score approximation (for full significance, use external stats library)
  ROUND((conversions::FLOAT/NULLIF(users,0)
    - MIN(conversions::FLOAT/NULLIF(users,0)) OVER ())
    / NULLIF(SQRT(MIN(conversions::FLOAT/NULLIF(users,0)) OVER ()
      * (1-MIN(conversions::FLOAT/NULLIF(users,0)) OVER ())/MIN(users) OVER ()), 0)
  , 3) AS approx_z_score
FROM experiment;

questions.question: Write a query to calculate customer lifetime value (LTV) by cohort.

blocks.source:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_month FROM orders GROUP BY 1
),
revenue AS (
  SELECT o.user_id, c.cohort_month,
    DATE_DIFF('month', c.cohort_month, DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)) AS months_since_join,
    SUM(o.total_amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN cohort c ON o.user_id=c.user_id
  GROUP BY 1,2,3
),
cohort_size AS (SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS sz FROM cohort GROUP BY 1)
SELECT r.cohort_month, cs.sz, r.months_since_join,
  SUM(SUM(r.revenue)) OVER (PARTITION BY r.cohort_month ORDER BY r.months_since_join) AS cumulative_revenue,
  ROUND(SUM(SUM(r.revenue)) OVER (PARTITION BY r.cohort_month ORDER BY r.months_since_join)/cs.sz, 2) AS ltv_per_user
FROM revenue r JOIN cohort_size cs ON r.cohort_month=cs.cohort_month
GROUP BY r.cohort_month, cs.sz, r.months_since_join ORDER BY r.cohort_month, r.months_since_join;

questions.question: Write a market basket analysis query — find products frequently bought together.

blocks.source:
SELECT a.product_id AS product_a, b.product_id AS product_b,
  COUNT(*) AS co_purchase_count,
  COUNT(*)::FLOAT / (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM orders) AS support
FROM order_items a
JOIN order_items b ON a.order_id=b.order_id AND a.product_id < b.product_id
GROUP BY a.product_id, b.product_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10
ORDER BY co_purchase_count DESC LIMIT 20;

questions.question: Write a query to compute revenue attribution — first touch vs last touch.

blocks.source:
WITH touches AS (
  SELECT user_id, channel, event_time,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time)     AS touch_num,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time DESC) AS touch_rev
  FROM marketing_touches
),
conversions AS (SELECT user_id, revenue FROM orders WHERE is_first_order=TRUE)
SELECT
  ft.channel AS first_touch_channel,
  lt.channel AS last_touch_channel,
  SUM(c.revenue) AS attributed_revenue,
  COUNT(*) AS conversions
FROM conversions c
JOIN touches ft ON c.user_id=ft.user_id AND ft.touch_num=1
JOIN touches lt ON c.user_id=lt.user_id AND lt.touch_rev=1
GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY attributed_revenue DESC;

questions.question: Write a user journey query — find the most common sequence of 3 consecutive events.

blocks.source:
WITH ordered_events AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_type, event_time,
    LEAD(event_type,1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS next_event,
    LEAD(event_type,2) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS next_next_event
  FROM events WHERE event_date >= CURRENT_DATE-7
)
SELECT event_type AS step1, next_event AS step2, next_next_event AS step3,
  COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM ordered_events
WHERE next_event IS NOT NULL AND next_next_event IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1,2,3
ORDER BY occurrences DESC LIMIT 10;

questions.question: Write a query to identify power users — top 10% of users by engagement score.

blocks.source:
WITH engagement AS (
  SELECT user_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT event_date)                    AS active_days,
    COUNT(*)                                       AS total_events,
    COUNT(DISTINCT event_type)                     AS event_types_used,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchases,
    -- Composite engagement score
    COUNT(DISTINCT event_date)*2 + COUNT(*)*0.1 + COUNT(DISTINCT event_type)*3 AS score
  FROM events WHERE event_date >= CURRENT_DATE-30
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT *, NTILE(10) OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS decile FROM engagement
) t WHERE decile=1 ORDER BY score DESC;

questions.question: Write a query to compute Day-7 rolling retention for each daily cohort.

blocks.source:
WITH cohorts AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_active FROM events GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  c.first_active AS cohort_date,
  COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id) AS cohort_size,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_date = c.first_active+7 THEN e.user_id END) AS retained_day7,
  ROUND(100.0*COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_date=c.first_active+7 THEN e.user_id END)/COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id),2) AS d7_retention_pct
FROM cohorts c
LEFT JOIN events e ON c.user_id=e.user_id AND e.event_date BETWEEN c.first_active AND c.first_active+7
WHERE c.first_active >= CURRENT_DATE-90
GROUP BY c.first_active ORDER BY c.first_active;

questions.question: Write a query to compute Net Promoter Score (NPS) from survey responses.

blocks.source:
-- NPS = % Promoters (9-10) - % Detractors (0-6)
WITH scores AS (
  SELECT survey_date, score,
    CASE WHEN score >= 9 THEN 'Promoter'
         WHEN score <= 6 THEN 'Detractor'
         ELSE 'Passive' END AS category
  FROM nps_surveys WHERE survey_date >= CURRENT_DATE-30
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_responses,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN category='Promoter'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),1) AS promoter_pct,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN category='Detractor' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),1) AS detractor_pct,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN category='Promoter'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*)
       -100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN category='Detractor' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*), 1) AS nps
FROM scores;

questions.question: Write a query to compute feature adoption rate — % of users who used each feature.

blocks.source:
SELECT feature_name,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)                                                    AS feature_users,
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM users WHERE created_at <= CURRENT_DATE) AS total_users,
  ROUND(100.0*COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)/

FROM feature_events
WHERE event_date >= CURRENT_DATE-30

questions.question: Write a query to build a customer health score using multiple weighted signals.

blocks.source:
WITH signals AS (
  SELECT c.customer_id,
    COALESCE(r.days_since_last_login, 999)  AS recency_days,
    COALESCE(u.logins_last_30d, 0)          AS login_frequency,
    COALESCE(p.features_used, 0)            AS product_depth,
    COALESCE(s.nps_score, 5)                AS satisfaction
  FROM customers c
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT user_id, CURRENT_DATE-MAX(login_date) AS days_since_last_login FROM logins GROUP BY 1) r ON c.customer_id=r.user_id
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS logins_last_30d FROM logins WHERE login_date>=CURRENT_DATE-30 GROUP BY 1) u ON c.customer_id=u.user_id
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT feature) AS features_used FROM feature_usage GROUP BY 1) p ON c.customer_id=p.customer_id
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, AVG(score) AS nps_score FROM nps_surveys GROUP BY 1) s ON c.customer_id=s.customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id,
  ROUND(
    (CASE WHEN recency_days < 7 THEN 30 WHEN recency_days < 30 THEN 20 ELSE 0 END)
    + LEAST(login_frequency*2, 30)
    + LEAST(product_depth*5, 30)
    + satisfaction
  ) AS health_score
FROM signals ORDER BY health_score DESC;

questions.question: Write a complete product analytics dashboard query — DAU, revenue, retention, top features.

    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_date BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE-7 AND CURRENT_DATE THEN e.user_id END) AS wau,

  LEFT JOIN users u    ON e.user_id=u.user_id
  WHERE e.event_date = CURRENT_DATE-1
)
SELECT * FROM daily;

questions.question: Amazon interview: Write a query to find the average delivery time by carrier and region, flagging carriers above the SLA.

blocks.source:
SELECT carrier, region,
  AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (delivered_at-shipped_at))/3600) AS avg_hours,
  COUNT(*) AS deliveries,
  CASE WHEN AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (delivered_at-shipped_at))/3600) > 48 THEN 'SLA BREACH' ELSE 'OK' END AS sla_status

questions.question: Uber interview: Write a query to detect surge pricing events — trips costing more than 2x the hourly average.

blocks.source:
WITH hourly_avg AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', trip_start) AS hr, AVG(fare_amount) AS avg_fare
  FROM trips GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT t.trip_id, t.trip_start, t.fare_amount, h.avg_fare,
  ROUND(t.fare_amount/NULLIF(h.avg_fare,0),2) AS fare_multiplier
FROM trips t
JOIN hourly_avg h ON DATE_TRUNC('hour', t.trip_start)=h.hr
WHERE t.fare_amount > h.avg_fare * 2
ORDER BY fare_multiplier DESC;

questions.question: Netflix interview: Write a query to compute content completion rate and identify shows with high drop-off.

blocks.source:
SELECT content_id, title, content_type,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)                           AS total_viewers,
  AVG(watch_pct)                                    AS avg_completion_pct,
  SUM(CASE WHEN watch_pct >= 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)  AS completions,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN watch_pct >= 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(DISTINCT user_id),1) AS completion_rate,
  AVG(CASE WHEN watch_pct < 10 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)*100 AS early_dropout_rate
FROM viewing_events v JOIN content c USING(content_id)
WHERE view_date >= CURRENT_DATE-7
GROUP BY content_id, title, content_type
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) > 100
ORDER BY completion_rate ASC LIMIT 20;

questions.question: Stripe interview: Write a query to detect potentially fraudulent transactions — multiple high-value transactions from the same IP in one hour.

blocks.source:
WITH hourly_activity AS (
  SELECT ip_address,
    DATE_TRUNC('hour', created_at) AS hr,
    COUNT(*) AS tx_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount,
    COUNT(DISTINCT card_fingerprint) AS distinct_cards
  FROM transactions
  WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE-1
  GROUP BY ip_address, DATE_TRUNC('hour', created_at)
)
SELECT ip_address, hr, tx_count, total_amount, distinct_cards,
  CASE WHEN tx_count >= 5 OR total_amount >= 10000 OR distinct_cards >= 3 THEN 'SUSPICIOUS' ELSE 'OK' END AS flag
FROM hourly_activity
WHERE tx_count >= 5 OR total_amount >= 10000 OR distinct_cards >= 3
ORDER BY total_amount DESC;

questions.question: LinkedIn interview: Write a query to compute connection graph density — avg connections per user and % with 500+ connections.

blocks.source:
WITH connection_counts AS (
  SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS connection_count
  FROM connections GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_users,
  ROUND(AVG(connection_count),1) AS avg_connections,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY connection_count) AS median_connections,
  MAX(connection_count) AS max_connections,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN connection_count >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS pct_500plus
FROM connection_counts;

questions.question: Airbnb interview: Write a query to find hosts with the highest occupancy rate in the last 90 days.

blocks.source:
WITH booking_days AS (
  SELECT listing_id,
    SUM(checkout_date - checkin_date) AS booked_days
  FROM bookings
  WHERE checkin_date >= CURRENT_DATE-90 AND status='confirmed'
  GROUP BY listing_id
)
SELECT l.listing_id, l.host_id, l.city,
  COALESCE(bd.booked_days, 0) AS booked_days,
  ROUND(100.0*COALESCE(bd.booked_days,0)/90, 1) AS occupancy_rate_pct
FROM listings l
LEFT JOIN booking_days bd ON l.listing_id=bd.listing_id
WHERE l.is_active=TRUE
ORDER BY occupancy_rate_pct DESC LIMIT 20;

questions.question: TikTok interview: Write a query to find videos that went viral — saw 10x view spike compared to creator's average.

blocks.source:
WITH creator_avg AS (
  SELECT creator_id, AVG(views_24h) AS avg_views FROM videos GROUP BY creator_id
)
SELECT v.video_id, v.creator_id, v.views_24h, ca.avg_views,
  ROUND(v.views_24h/NULLIF(ca.avg_views,0),1) AS views_vs_avg_multiplier
FROM videos v JOIN creator_avg ca ON v.creator_id=ca.creator_id
WHERE v.views_24h > ca.avg_views*10
  AND v.published_at >= CURRENT_DATE-7
ORDER BY views_vs_avg_multiplier DESC;

questions.question: Shopify interview: Write a query to identify stores at risk of churning — declining GMV 3 months in a row.

blocks.source:
WITH monthly_gmv AS (
  SELECT store_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS mo, SUM(gmv) AS monthly_gmv
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1,2
),
trend AS (
  SELECT store_id, mo, monthly_gmv,
    LAG(monthly_gmv,1) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY mo) AS m1_ago,
    LAG(monthly_gmv,2) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY mo) AS m2_ago
  FROM monthly_gmv
)
SELECT store_id, mo, monthly_gmv, m1_ago, m2_ago
FROM trend
WHERE mo = DATE_TRUNC('month', CURRENT_DATE)
  AND monthly_gmv < m1_ago AND m1_ago < m2_ago  -- 3 consecutive declining months
ORDER BY monthly_gmv ASC;

questions.question: Snowflake: Write a query using MERGE for a full SCD Type 2 upsert in one statement.

blocks.source:
MERGE INTO dim_customer AS target
USING staging_customers AS source ON target.customer_id=source.customer_id AND target.is_current=TRUE
WHEN MATCHED AND (
  source.email IS DISTINCT FROM target.email OR source.city IS DISTINCT FROM target.city
) THEN
  UPDATE SET target.is_current=FALSE, target.eff_to=CURRENT_DATE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (customer_id, email, city, eff_from, is_current)
  VALUES (source.customer_id, source.email, source.city, CURRENT_DATE, TRUE);

-- Insert new versions for changed records (after MERGE closes old rows)
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_id, email, city, eff_from, is_current)
SELECT s.customer_id, s.email, s.city, CURRENT_DATE, TRUE
FROM staging_customers s JOIN dim_customer d
  ON s.customer_id=d.customer_id AND d.eff_to=CURRENT_DATE AND d.is_current=FALSE;

questions.question: BigQuery: Write a query to compute user engagement scores using ML.BUCKETIZE for scoring.

  ML.BUCKETIZE(days_since_last_active, [7,14,30,60,90]) AS recency_bucket,
  ML.BUCKETIZE(sessions_last_30d, [1,3,7,15,30]) AS frequency_bucket,
  ML.BUCKETIZE(total_revenue, [10,50,200,500,1000]) AS monetary_bucket
FROM (

    COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions_last_30d,
    SUM(purchase_amount) AS total_revenue
  FROM `project.dataset.events`
  WHERE event_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE, INTERVAL 30 DAY)
  GROUP BY user_id
);

questions.question: Write a recursive CTE to find all descendants in an org chart.

blocks.source:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  -- Anchor: start from a specific manager
  SELECT employee_id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth, name AS path
  FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 100  -- root manager
  UNION ALL
  -- Recursive: find all reports
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth+1,
    o.path || ' → ' || e.name
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id=o.employee_id
)
SELECT employee_id, name, depth, path FROM org ORDER BY path;

questions.question: Write a query to compute median and percentiles without built-in functions.

blocks.source:
-- Manual percentile calculation using ROW_NUMBER
SELECT
  AVG(salary) AS mean_salary,
  -- P50 (median)
  AVG(CASE WHEN rn IN (CEIL(cnt/2.0), FLOOR(cnt/2.0)+1) THEN salary END) AS median_salary,
  -- P25
  AVG(CASE WHEN rn = CEIL(cnt*0.25) THEN salary END) AS p25_salary,
  -- P75
  AVG(CASE WHEN rn = CEIL(cnt*0.75) THEN salary END) AS p75_salary,
  -- P90
  AVG(CASE WHEN rn = CEIL(cnt*0.90) THEN salary END) AS p90_salary
FROM (
  SELECT salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS rn, COUNT(*) OVER () AS cnt
  FROM employees
) t;

questions.question: Write a query to detect user account sharing — same account logged in from different IPs concurrently.

blocks.source:
SELECT a.user_id, a.session_id AS session_a, b.session_id AS session_b,
  a.ip_address AS ip_a, b.ip_address AS ip_b,
  a.login_time, b.login_time AS b_login_time
FROM user_sessions a
JOIN user_sessions b
  ON a.user_id=b.user_id
  AND a.session_id < b.session_id
  AND a.ip_address != b.ip_address              -- different IPs
  AND a.login_time < COALESCE(b.logout_time, NOW())  -- overlapping sessions
  AND b.login_time < COALESCE(a.logout_time, NOW())
ORDER BY a.user_id, a.login_time;

questions.question: Write a query that uses a covering index — select only indexed columns to avoid table lookups.

blocks.source:
-- Table: orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, total_amount, notes)
-- Covering index: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_covering ON orders(order_date, status, total_amount);

-- This query can be satisfied entirely from the index (no heap access)
SELECT order_date, status, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31'
  AND status = 'completed'
GROUP BY order_date, status;

-- AVOID: selecting 'notes' forces a heap lookup even with the index
-- SELECT order_date, status, total_amount, notes FROM orders WHERE ...

blocks.label: Stackle Tip
blocks.html: A covering index contains all columns needed by a query, eliminating the need to go back to the table. This can make queries 10-100x faster on large tables.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Hash Join, Merge Join, and Nested Loop Join?

blocks.html: Nested Loop Join — for each row in the outer table, scan the inner table. O(n×m). Best when inner table is small or heavily indexed. Common in OLTP.
Hash Join — build a hash table on the smaller table, probe with the larger. O(n+m). Best for large unsorted tables with no useful index. Most common in analytics.
Merge Join — both inputs are sorted, then merged. O(n log n + m log m). Best when both sides are pre-sorted (e.g., by a clustered index). Very efficient when data is already ordered.

blocks.source:
-- PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN shows which join type is chosen
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-01-01';

questions.question: Write a query to find the most expensive queries in a PostgreSQL database using pg_stat_statements.

blocks.source:
SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time/1000 AS total_sec,
  mean_exec_time/1000 AS mean_sec,
  rows, 100.0*shared_blks_hit/NULLIF(shared_blks_hit+shared_blks_read,0) AS cache_hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 20;

blocks.label: Stackle Tip
blocks.html: pg_stat_statements is the first thing to check when investigating slow databases. Sort by total_exec_time to find what's costing the most cumulative time, not just the slowest individual query.

questions.question: What are the main causes of slow queries, and how do you diagnose them?

blocks.html: Key causes: missing indexes (full table scans), bad join order, functions on indexed columns preventing index use, large intermediate result sets, N+1 query patterns, lock contention, statistics out of date.

blocks.source:
-- Diagnose with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE LOWER(status) = 'completed'; -- BAD: function prevents index use

-- Fix: use expression index OR change query
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(LOWER(status)); -- expression index
-- OR: store status consistently uppercased and query as:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'; -- index used

questions.question: Write a query to rewrite a correlated subquery as a window function for performance.

blocks.source:
-- SLOW: correlated subquery runs once per row
SELECT employee_id, salary,
  (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department = e1.department) AS dept_avg
FROM employees e1;

-- FAST: window function scans once
SELECT employee_id, salary,
  AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
FROM employees;

blocks.label: Stackle Tip
blocks.html: Replacing correlated subqueries with window functions is one of the highest-impact SQL optimizations. Always look for this pattern in slow query reviews.

questions.question: Write a query to rewrite a NOT IN as NOT EXISTS for better NULL safety and performance.

blocks.source:
-- RISKY: NOT IN with NULLs returns no rows if any value is NULL
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items); -- fails if any NULL in subquery!

-- SAFE and often faster: NOT EXISTS
SELECT * FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id
);

-- Also safe: LEFT JOIN + IS NULL
SELECT p.* FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL;

questions.question: Write a query to use partial indexes to speed up queries on a specific subset.

blocks.source:
-- Only index active orders (partial index)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_active ON orders(customer_id, order_date)
WHERE status = 'active';

-- Query will use this index when filtering on active orders
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 12345 AND status = 'active'
ORDER BY order_date DESC;

-- The partial index is smaller (fewer rows indexed) → faster scans, less memory
-- Great for tables with a dominant 'archived' or 'deleted' status that you rarely query

questions.question: Write a query using materialized CTEs to force intermediate materialization in PostgreSQL.

blocks.source:
-- PostgreSQL 12+: CTEs are inlined by default (optimizer can transform them)
-- Force materialization to prevent the optimizer from re-running the CTE multiple times:
WITH expensive_calc AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT product_id, SUM(revenue) AS total_rev
  FROM sales WHERE sale_date >= '2024-01-01'
  GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT p.product_name, ec.total_rev
FROM expensive_calc ec
JOIN products p ON ec.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE ec.total_rev > 10000;

questions.question: Write a query to compare execution plans for two alternative query approaches.

blocks.source:
-- Compare two approaches side by side
-- Approach 1: subquery
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON)
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE country = 'US');

-- Approach 2: JOIN
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON)
SELECT o.* FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.country = 'US';

-- Check: actual rows, actual time, loops, shared blocks read
-- Cheaper plan = fewer blocks read + lower actual time

questions.question: Write a query to analyze index usage — find unused indexes wasting disk space.

blocks.source:
-- PostgreSQL: find indexes that are never (or rarely) used
SELECT
  schemaname,
  tablename,
  indexname,
  idx_scan AS times_used,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexname::regclass)) AS index_size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0  -- never used
  AND indexname NOT LIKE '%pkey%'  -- keep PKs
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexname::regclass) DESC;

blocks.label: Stackle Tip
blocks.html: Unused indexes waste disk space, slow down writes, and consume buffer cache. Dropping them can significantly improve write performance on high-volume tables.

questions.question: What is query plan caching and when does it cause performance problems?

blocks.html: Databases cache (reuse) query execution plans for parameterized queries. The first execution chooses a plan based on statistics. Problems occur when:
1. Parameter sniffing — plan optimized for first parameter value performs poorly for different values (e.g., plan for user_id=1 with 10K orders is bad for user_id=2 with 1 order).
2. Stale statistics — statistics used to choose the plan are outdated after bulk loads.

questions.question: Write a query using table partitioning to demonstrate partition pruning.
Write a query using EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify a sequential scan that should be an index scan.

blocks.source:
-- Check if a query uses an index or does a full table scan
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345;

/*
Expected output if no index exists:
  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..1842.00 rows=1 width=200)
    Filter: (customer_id = 12345)
    Rows Removed by Filter: 99999
    Buffers: shared hit=842

Expected output WITH index:
  Index Scan using idx_orders_customer_id on orders
    Index Cond: (customer_id = 12345)
    Buffers: shared hit=4  ← much fewer blocks read!
*/

-- Fix: create the missing index
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders(customer_id);

questions.question: Write a query to demonstrate the difference between index scan and bitmap index scan.

blocks.source:
-- Index Scan: best for highly selective queries (few rows)
-- Fetches rows one at a time from the heap in index order
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = 99999; -- PK lookup

-- Bitmap Index Scan: best for moderate selectivity (many rows, but <5% of table)
-- Builds a bitmap of matching heap pages, then fetches them in physical order
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND order_date >= '2024-01-01';
-- May combine: BitmapAnd(bitmap_scan_status, bitmap_scan_date)

-- Sequential Scan: best when returning most of the table
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status != 'cancelled'; -- returns 99%

questions.question: Write a query to measure and reduce bloat in a frequently updated PostgreSQL table.

blocks.source:
-- Check table bloat (dead tuples from UPDATEs/DELETEs)
SELECT
  relname AS table_name,
  n_dead_tup AS dead_tuples,
  n_live_tup AS live_tuples,
  ROUND(100.0 * n_dead_tup / NULLIF(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0), 2) AS bloat_pct,
  last_vacuum, last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_dead_tup > 10000
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

-- Fix: VACUUM removes dead tuples, VACUUM FULL reclaims disk space
VACUUM orders;           -- non-blocking, reclaims space for reuse
VACUUM FULL orders;      -- locks table, returns space to OS
ANALYZE orders;          -- update statistics for query planner

questions.question: Write a query to implement a slowly changing dimension Type 1 (overwrite in place).

blocks.source:
-- SCD Type 1: just UPDATE the record (no history kept)
UPDATE dim_customer
SET
  email   = s.email,
  city    = s.city,
  updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
FROM staging_customers s
WHERE dim_customer.customer_id = s.customer_id
  AND (
    dim_customer.email IS DISTINCT FROM s.email
    OR dim_customer.city IS DISTINCT FROM s.city
  );

-- Or as UPSERT (handle new records too)
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_id, email, city, updated_at)
SELECT customer_id, email, city, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP FROM staging_customers
ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO UPDATE
  SET email=EXCLUDED.email, city=EXCLUDED.city, updated_at=EXCLUDED.updated_at;

questions.question: Write a query implementing a bridge table for a many-to-many relationship.

blocks.source:
-- Bridge/junction table: orders to promotions (many-to-many)
CREATE TABLE order_promotions (
  order_id    INTEGER REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  promo_id    INTEGER REFERENCES promotions(promo_id),
  applied_at  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  discount_amount NUMERIC(10,2),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, promo_id)
);

-- Query: total discount per promotion
SELECT p.promo_code, p.description,
  COUNT(op.order_id) AS orders_used,
  SUM(op.discount_amount) AS total_discount
FROM promotions p
JOIN order_promotions op ON p.promo_id = op.promo_id
GROUP BY p.promo_id, p.promo_code, p.description
ORDER BY total_discount DESC;

questions.question: Write a query to compute a 'rolling 30-day unique users' metric efficiently.

blocks.source:
-- Each day: how many distinct users were active in the trailing 30 days?
SELECT d.calendar_date,
  COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_id) AS rolling_30d_users
FROM dim_date d
JOIN events e ON e.event_date BETWEEN d.calendar_date-29 AND d.calendar_date
WHERE d.calendar_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
GROUP BY d.calendar_date
ORDER BY d.calendar_date;

-- Note: COUNT(DISTINCT) inside a window function is NOT supported in most databases
-- This JOIN approach is the standard workaround

questions.question: Write a query to implement 'top N per group with tie handling' — show ties at the boundary.

blocks.source:
-- Show top 3 products per category, but include ALL ties at position 3
SELECT category, product_id, product_name, revenue, rank_in_cat
FROM (
  SELECT
    p.category, p.product_id, p.product_name,
    SUM(s.revenue) AS revenue,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY SUM(s.revenue) DESC) AS rank_in_cat
  FROM sales s JOIN products p ON s.product_id = p.product_id
  GROUP BY p.category, p.product_id, p.product_name
) t
WHERE rank_in_cat <= 3  -- DENSE_RANK includes ties; RANK skips numbers after ties; ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily
ORDER BY category, rank_in_cat;

questions.question: Write a query to build a calendar spine — every date with metrics, filling in zeros for missing days.

blocks.source:
WITH date_spine AS (
  SELECT generate_series::DATE AS dt
  FROM generate_series('2024-01-01'::DATE, '2024-12-31'::DATE, '1 day'::INTERVAL)
)
SELECT ds.dt,
  COALESCE(dm.revenue, 0) AS revenue,
  COALESCE(dm.orders, 0)  AS orders
FROM date_spine ds
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT DATE(order_date) AS dt, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS orders
  FROM orders GROUP BY DATE(order_date)
) dm ON ds.dt = dm.dt
ORDER BY ds.dt;

blocks.label: Stackle Tip
blocks.html: A date spine is essential for time-series analysis — without it, missing days are silently dropped, causing gaps in charts and incorrect moving averages.

questions.question: Write a query to implement optimistic locking — detect and reject concurrent conflicting updates.

blocks.source:
-- Optimistic locking using a version column
CREATE TABLE inventory (
  product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  quantity   INTEGER,
  version    INTEGER DEFAULT 1
);

-- Application reads: SELECT product_id, quantity, version FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 1
-- Application stores version=5 locally

-- Application update (includes version check):
UPDATE inventory
SET quantity = quantity - 1,
    version  = version + 1
WHERE product_id = 1
  AND version = 5;  -- only succeeds if no one else updated since we read

-- If 0 rows updated → conflict detected → retry or reject

questions.question: Write a query that demonstrates the difference between UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT.

blocks.source:
-- UNION: all rows from both (deduped)
SELECT customer_id FROM 2023_customers
UNION
SELECT customer_id FROM 2024_customers;

-- UNION ALL: all rows including duplicates (faster)
SELECT customer_id FROM 2023_customers
UNION ALL
SELECT customer_id FROM 2024_customers;

-- INTERSECT: only rows in BOTH
SELECT customer_id FROM 2023_customers
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM 2024_customers;  -- retained customers

-- EXCEPT: rows in first but NOT second
SELECT customer_id FROM 2023_customers
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM 2024_customers;  -- churned customers

questions.question: Write a query to use GROUPING SETS for a multi-level summary report.

blocks.source:
SELECT
  COALESCE(region, 'ALL REGIONS')           AS region,
  COALESCE(product_category, 'ALL CATEGORIES') AS category,
  SUM(revenue) AS revenue
FROM sales
WHERE sale_date >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
  (region, product_category),  -- subtotal by region+category
  (region),                    -- subtotal by region only
  ()                           -- grand total
)
ORDER BY region NULLS LAST, category NULLS LAST;

-- Equivalent to: GROUP BY region, category UNION ALL GROUP BY region UNION ALL SELECT total
-- But in ONE scan of the data — much more efficient

questions.question: Write a query to implement a priority queue — process tasks by priority and insertion order.

blocks.source:
-- Task queue with priority (lower number = higher priority)
SELECT task_id, task_name, priority, created_at, status
FROM tasks
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY priority ASC, created_at ASC  -- primary: priority, tiebreak: FIFO
LIMIT 10;  -- claim next 10 tasks

-- Atomic claim (prevent two workers from taking same task)
UPDATE tasks
SET status='in_progress', claimed_at=NOW(), worker_id=:worker_id
WHERE task_id IN (
  SELECT task_id FROM tasks WHERE status='pending'
  ORDER BY priority ASC, created_at ASC LIMIT 1
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED  -- skip tasks locked by other workers
)
RETURNING *;

questions.question: Write a query to implement a token bucket algorithm for rate limiting in SQL.

blocks.source:
-- Track token consumption per user
-- Bucket refills at 10 tokens/minute, max 50 tokens
WITH current_tokens AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    tokens_remaining,
    last_refill,
    -- Refill tokens based on time since last refill
    LEAST(50,
      tokens_remaining + FLOOR(
        EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW()-last_refill))/60 * 10  -- 10 tokens per minute
      )
    ) AS available_tokens
  FROM rate_limit_buckets WHERE user_id = :user_id
)
UPDATE rate_limit_buckets
SET tokens_remaining = CASE WHEN ct.available_tokens >= 1 THEN ct.available_tokens-1 ELSE ct.available_tokens END,
    last_refill = CASE WHEN ct.available_tokens >= 1 THEN NOW() ELSE last_refill END
FROM current_tokens ct
WHERE rate_limit_buckets.user_id = ct.user_id
RETURNING tokens_remaining >= 1 AS request_allowed;

questions.question: Write a query to compute a 'lag fill' — for each record, find the closest prior value in a sparse table.

blocks.source:
-- For each date, find the most recent non-null price (even if days apart)
SELECT product_id, price_date, price,
  MAX(price) OVER (
    PARTITION BY product_id,
    -- Group consecutive NULLs with the preceding non-null value
    COUNT(price) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY price_date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
    ORDER BY price_date
  ) AS filled_price
FROM product_daily_prices
ORDER BY product_id, price_date;

-- If your database supports IGNORE NULLS:
-- LAST_VALUE(price IGNORE NULLS) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY price_date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)

questions.question: Write a query to compute running total that resets at each category boundary.

blocks.source:
SELECT
  category,
  sale_date,
  daily_revenue,
  SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (
    PARTITION BY category            -- reset at each category
    ORDER BY sale_date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS category_ytd_revenue
FROM daily_sales_by_category
ORDER BY category, sale_date;

questions.question: Write a query to flatten a parent-child hierarchy into breadcrumb paths.

blocks.source:
WITH RECURSIVE breadcrumb AS (
  -- Leaf nodes: start with the deepest categories
  SELECT category_id, parent_id, name, name AS path, 0 AS depth
  FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.category_id, c.parent_id, c.name,
    b.path || ' > ' || c.name AS path,
    b.depth + 1
  FROM categories c JOIN breadcrumb b ON c.parent_id = b.category_id
)
SELECT category_id, name, depth, path
FROM breadcrumb
ORDER BY path;

-- Example output:
-- Electronics
-- Electronics > Phones
-- Electronics > Phones > Smartphones
-- Electronics > Computers

questions.question: Write a query to implement a 'lead generation scoring' model using weighted SQL signals.

blocks.source:
WITH signals AS (
  SELECT
    lead_id,
    -- Behavioral signals (out of 100)
    LEAST(page_views * 2, 20)                                AS page_score,
    CASE WHEN downloaded_whitepaper THEN 15 ELSE 0 END       AS download_score,
    CASE WHEN attended_webinar THEN 20 ELSE 0 END            AS webinar_score,
    CASE WHEN requested_demo THEN 30 ELSE 0 END              AS demo_score,
    -- Firmographic signals (out of 100)
    CASE WHEN company_size > 1000 THEN 15
         WHEN company_size > 100  THEN 10 ELSE 5 END         AS size_score,
    CASE WHEN industry IN ('Finance','Healthcare') THEN 15 ELSE 5 END AS industry_score
  FROM leads l
  LEFT JOIN lead_activities la ON l.lead_id = la.lead_id
)
SELECT lead_id,
  (page_score+download_score+webinar_score+demo_score+size_score+industry_score) AS total_score,
  CASE WHEN (page_score+download_score+webinar_score+demo_score+size_score+industry_score) >= 70 THEN 'Hot'
       WHEN (page_score+download_score+webinar_score+demo_score+size_score+industry_score) >= 40 THEN 'Warm'
       ELSE 'Cold' END AS lead_grade
FROM signals ORDER BY total_score DESC;

questions.question: Write a comprehensive query combining window functions, CTEs, JOINs, and aggregations to produce a complete customer 360 view.

blocks.source:
WITH customer_orders AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
    SUM(total_amount) AS lifetime_value,
    AVG(total_amount) AS avg_order_value,
    MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date,
    MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date,
    CURRENT_DATE - MAX(order_date)::DATE AS days_since_last_order
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
),
customer_segments AS (
  SELECT customer_id, lifetime_value,
    NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC) AS value_quartile,
    CASE
      WHEN days_since_last_order <= 30  THEN 'Active'
      WHEN days_since_last_order <= 90  THEN 'At Risk'
      WHEN days_since_last_order <= 180 THEN 'Lapsing'
      ELSE 'Churned'
    END AS lifecycle_stage
  FROM customer_orders
),
favorite_category AS (
  SELECT oi.customer_id_ref AS customer_id, p.category,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY oi.customer_id_ref ORDER BY SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) DESC) AS cat_rank
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id=oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id=p.product_id
  GROUP BY oi.customer_id_ref, p.category
)
SELECT
  c.customer_id, c.name, c.email, c.country,
  co.total_orders, co.lifetime_value, co.avg_order_value,
  co.first_order_date, co.last_order_date, co.days_since_last_order,
  cs.lifecycle_stage,
  CASE cs.value_quartile WHEN 1 THEN 'Platinum' WHEN 2 THEN 'Gold' WHEN 3 THEN 'Silver' ELSE 'Bronze' END AS value_tier,
  fc.category AS favorite_category
FROM customers c
JOIN customer_orders co ON c.customer_id=co.customer_id
JOIN customer_segments cs ON c.customer_id=cs.customer_id
LEFT JOIN favorite_category fc ON c.customer_id=fc.customer_id AND fc.cat_rank=1
ORDER BY co.lifetime_value DESC;

blocks.label: Stackle Tip
blocks.html: This is a senior-level query pattern. Being able to build a comprehensive customer 360 view — combining lifecycle stage, value tier, recency, and preferences — in one clean CTE chain shows you understand both SQL and business analytics deeply.
